Parks Commission Recreation - Report 1/15/2025 Senior Programs: Active and Aging The Aging & Active program returned from Thanksgiving break and started to prepare for their next Holiday Christmas. West Central held a bean Bag Baseball All-Star Game on December 5, along with polish sausage chili day. East Little Rock & Southwest celebrated the holiday on December 20. East Little Rock, Southwest & Stephens Community Centers These centers are under renovations and will be updated with flooring, lights and an overall brighter and appealing look. Therapeutic Recreation The month of December we had our Annual Therapeutic Recreation Christmas Program, it was held at Fellowship Bible Church in partnership with their Embrace Special Needs Ministry on December 19, we had a cast of 21 participants for this performance. Southwest Community Center Our cheerleaders continue to shine in the community, they participated in the Annual Southwest Christmas Parade on Saturday December 7, 2024. On December 5, 2024, we partnered with the Pulaski County Lawyer Association to provide a free service to those in need of clearing their records, over 250 participants attended. MacArthur Museum of Military History On-site visitation included 458 walk-in guests and 204 visitors to special events, tours, etc. during the month. In addition to Arkansas, guests came from 20 states – as well as six foreign countries – Brazil, Canada, Ecuador, Germany, India, and South Korea. Outdoor Recreation Work has begun on mapping and layout for a new disc golf at Reservoir Park. First–Tee Golf Although we experienced some slower periods this month, we have successfully maintained the golf course by clearing leaves and conducting tree trimming. Additionally, we promoted gift card sales for the upcoming holiday season. As we approach the end of the year, we are eagerly anticipating the 2025 golf season and the opportunities it will bring, including the introduction of new participants in this cherished sport. Youth Athletics Youth Basketball Season starts next month, registration is still going on at each location, the goal was to have at least 350 youth registered and to date there are 360. 1 Parks Commission – Recreation Report 1/15/2025 Dunbar Community Center After School Programs The after-school program at Dunbar Community Center wrapped up this month. Youth enjoyed our annual holiday meal on December 13th and received gifts from the center. Gifts included stuffed animals, games of their choice and Christmas pencils. Staff was on hand to keep the youth safe and interacted with them in pick-up basketball. Special Event We hosted a Christmas paint party which was opened to anyone who wanted to attend. Fruit bags were gifted to all who came, and Christmas music played in the background. The Afterschool Program had a great Christmas party on December 12, 2024. We gave the kids a snack bag with jellybeans in a Christmas ornament, apples, and oranges. Bylaws of the Little Rock Parks and Recreation Advisory Commission Article I - Name The name of the Commission shall be the Little Rock Parks and Recreation Commission ("Commission"). Article II- Purpose Intent. The Commission was created to review, consult and advise tbe City on matters concerning the operation and maintenance of the Parks and Recreation Department and the implementation of the master parks plan. Pursuant to the ordinance that created the Commission, significant issues involving or affecting these matters shall be referred to and considered by Commission prior to consideration by the Little Rock Board of Directors. The intent of these bylaws to formalize tbe organization of the Commission, provide the process to conduct its affairs, and to keep records of Commission proceedings for the use and benefit of tbe general public. Responsibilities. The Commission shall have the following responsibilities pursuant to Little Rock, Ark. Rev. Code ("LRC") §2-330 (1988): (a) To hold periodic meetings not less tban once a month, which are open to the public and for which minutes shall be maintained; (b) To consult with and advise the director of Little Rock Parks and Recreation, and to recommend policies and plans for the operation, maintenance and expansion of the park system, facilities and programs; (c) In consultation with the director of Little Rock Parks and Recreation Department (the "Director"), to recommend to the city manager park land and facility acquisitions based on the criteria contained in the Asset Management and Disposition Policy for Little Rock Parks and Recreation Park Land adopted by the board of directors; (d) In consultation with the Director, to recommend fees, rates, tolls, and charges for the services, facilities and commodities rendered by the properties and programs of the park system; (e) In consultation with the Director, to recommend rules and regulations governing the use and protection of the park system and property therein; (f) To consult with and advise the Director on the master parks plan and the best approach for implementation, including but not limited to prioritizing projects and recommending capital funding allocations; (g) To consult with and advise the Director on an annual basis regarding the determination of the financial needs for the Parks Department and to report these budget needs for the next year to the city manager for possible inclusion in the City's budget process, provided that any budget recommendation will assure that the City's covenants pursuant to any outstanding parks and recreation revenue bonds are met; (h) To submit an annual report to the Little Rock Board of Directors that addresses the state of the operations, facilities and programs of Little Rock Parks and Recreation Department; (i) To cooperate with counties, municipalities and other political subdivisions of the state on matters relating to planning, establishing, developing, improving or maintaining any park, parkway or recreational area that has an impact beyond the city limits; G) To have all authority, subordinate to the Little Rock Board of Directors, or the city manager, which is not specifically enumerated in the ordinance that created the Commission, to operate and improve the city's park system, facilities and programs, provided that such authority does not violate or conflict with state law, subject to the city or any of its employees to liability, or is contrary to the covenants of any outstanding bond issues. Article III - Membership Membership and Terms. The membership shall consist ofno fewer than five (5) and no more than eleven (11) residents of Little Rock, Arkansas, who will serve three-year terms. The Director or his or her designee, shall serve as an ex-officio member of the Commission and work closely with the Commission by attending all meetings and providing information about Parks Department projects and programs. Vacancies on the Commission shall be filled by appointments made by the Commission which must be affirmed by the Little Rock Board of Directors. The Commission may from time to time elect honorary life members, as it deems appropriate. Compensation. Members shall serve without compensation but may be reimbursed for expenses necessarily incurred in the performance of Commission business in accordance with city policy and Arkansas law. Attendance. Commission members are expected to attend all meetings to ensure the existence of a quorum in order to conduct business. When a member has missed more than twenty-five (25) percent of all regular meetings of the Commission in one (1) calendar year or more than three (3) consecutive regularly scheduled meetings, the member is automatically removed from the -2- Commission. The Commission shall immediately certify to the city manager that the member has missed the requisite number of meetings. If, prior to the next scheduled meeting of the City Board of Directors, the member submits in writing his or her desire to remain on the Commission, the Board of Directors, by a majority vote, may allow the member to continue to serve. If the member is not allowed to continue to serve on the Commission, the vacancy shall be filled according to the applicable provisions of the Little Rock City Code. Article IV - Officers and their Selection Officers, The officers of the Parks and Recreation Commission shall consist of a Chair, a Vice Chair and a Secretary. The Chair and Vice Chair shall serve in their elected position for one (1) year. The Director, or his her designee, shall serve as the Secretary to the Commission. Elections. The Commission shall nominate and elect the Chair and Vice Chair at its first meeting of each calendar year. Duties. Duties of the Chair: • • • • Preside at all meetings. Make committee appointments. Work closely with the Department. Carry out other duties as assigned by the Commission. Duties of the Vice-Chair: • In the absence of the chair, serve in his or her capacity. Duties of the Secretary: • • • Plan agenda with the input of chair and any interested parties. Distribute minutes and agendas to all Commission, Administration, and Board of Directors members no less than one (I) week prior to the regularly scheduled Commission meeting. Attend 1111 meetings and record all activities in the form of minutes. Article VI - Meetings Open Meetings. All meetings of the Commission shall be open to the public as required by the Arkansas Freedom oflnformation Act. Regular Meetings. At its last regular meeting of each calendar year, the Commission shall adopt a calendar of regular meeting dates for the forthcoming year for submission to the City Clerk's Office. Regular meetings of the Commission shall be held each month in a location designated in the adopted calendar. Regular meetings may be postponed or rescheduled by the Secretary for -3- lack of a quorum; or rescheduled for other reasonable cause approved by a two-thirds (2/3) majority vote of the Commission members present at a regular meeting, provided at least five (5) days' notice of the rescheduled time is given to all commission members, to the Parks Department, and to the Little Rock Public Relations Manager for purposes of providing Freedom of Information Act notice. Special Meetings. Special meetings may be called by the Chair upon ten (10) days written notice of the time, date, location and purpose of the meeting to all Commission members, to the Parks Department, and to the Little Rock Public Relations Manager for purposes of providing Freedom of Information Act notice. Special meetings may be called by a two-thirds (2/3) majority vote of the members present at any regular meeting. Ten (10) days written notice of the time, date, location and purpose of the meeting shall be sent to all commission members, to the Department, and to the Little Rock Public Relations Manager for purposes of providing Freedom oflnformation Act notice. Public Hearings. When the Commission is to hold a public hearing on parks regulations, parks ordinances, amendments to ordinances or regulations, or other parks and recreation matters for which citizen input is helpful or appropriate, notice of the hearing may be published at least one time in a newspaper having general circulation throughout the City of Little Rock at least fifteen (15) days prior to the hearing. The notice shall contain the time, date, location and purpose of the hearing. If the matter before the Commission involves a particular piece of property, a courtesy notice shall be sent by regular mail postage prepaid at least fifteen (15) days before the hearing to each resident and each known owner of property within any identifiable area of impact, as determined by the Director Public hearings shall be conducted informally, and the Chair shall be in charge of the meeting. It shall be the purpose of the hearing to obtain information on essential matters while entertaining the presentation of contrary positions to do substantial justice to all concerned. No request to discuss an issue or issues at a public hearing which is not docketed may be acted upon by the Commission. Once the Commission approves a recommendation on an issue for the City Board of Directors, no subsequent hearing on such recommendation shall be held unless requested by the Board or the City Manager. Quorum. Attendance of a majority oCthe voting members serving on the Commission shall constitute a quorum. Business may be conducted only in meetings in which a quorum is present. Voting. All questions submitted by the Commission for decision shall be determined by a viva voce vote of present and voting Commission members. The Chairman shall cast the last vote on any issue. A roll call vote shall be taken upon the request of any member of the Commission. No Commissioner shall cast a vote for another member of the Commission by proxy. -4- A majority vote shall be required for all actions or recommendations by the Commission except where a specific rule provides otherwise. A majority vote is defined as votes cast by more than half of the members in attendance. Conflict of Interest, Members of the Commission shall disclose any matters that (to their knowledge) would have a direct or indirect financial impact on them or their relatives, as distinguished from the public generally. The fact that there is such an interest shall be disclosed to the Commission no later than the first Commission meeting at which the matter is to be taken up for consideration, recommendation, discussion or vote. The Secretary shall make a record of such disclosure in the minutes of the Commission. After the Commission member determines that he or she has a conflict of interest (and once all conflict of interest questions have been resolved), the member shall remove himself or herself from the meeting room or area of the room occupied by the general public and shall not return to his or her seat until the deliberation and action on the item is completed. Any member may request an informal opinion from the City Attorney as to whether a conflict of interest exists in a particular case. The minutes shall show each exact motion; who offered the motion; who seconded the motion; and how each member voted. On-site visits included 365 walk-in guests and 281 visitors to special events, tours, etc. during the month. In addition to Arkansas, guests came from Arizona, California, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas and Wisconsin, as well as from Canada, England, Germany, Japan and Switzerland. Two Minutes to Midnight and the Architecture of Armageddon, a traveling exhibit from Exhibits USA and Mid-America Arts Alliance in Kansas City, MO was de-installed on January 9 and shipped to its next venue in Wyoming. The exhibit draws attention to individual children and communities affected by war. Children often share their experiences and emotions through indirect methods of communication such as art and play. In the exhibit, internationally recognized photographer Brian McCarty collaborates with children who have been affected by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The museum has received a historical marker commemorating the contributions of African American soldiers in the Civil War. The cost of the marker was funded from a grant from the Arkansas Historical Marker Program as well as a private donor. Museum supervisor Stephan McAteer participated in a podcast with Amanda Williams, the director of the MacArthur Memorial in Norfolk, VA on January 21. The podcast focused on Douglas MacArthur's birth in the Arsenal Building on January 26, 1880, and was used by the Memorial to commemorate the general's birthday. This month, we met with the Parks Director to discuss how we would like to utilize the funds allocated from the bond money set aside for golf. We have begun the process of ordering new equipment for both golf courses. Additionally, we are looking to build a cart barn/pavilion storage area here at First Tee. One of the design aspects we want to incorporate is an open structure, allowing customers to walk in and retrieve a golf cart easily. This setup would help reduce costs associated with part-time salaries for facility staff. Furthermore, we are planning to initiate a two-phase installation of cart paths on the golf course. Finalizing a contract for a leased golf cart for our maintenance crew. Museum of Arkansas Military History Museum attendance for February (through 2/26) was 1,611. This number included: (1) on-site visitation, (2) special events, (3) virtual programming through the museum's mini-documentaries and interviews, and (4) off-site programming and outreach. On-site visits included 446 walk-in guests and 365 visitors to special events, tours, etc. during the month. In addition to Arkansas, guests came from Alabama, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, 6 and Virginia as well as from France, Peru, South Korea and Spain. The museum's virtual documentaries/interviews received 574 new views during February. During February, museum staff presented weekly programming to 87 students at Dunbar Community Center and 63 students at Stephens Community Center as part of the After School Program. Another 76 students were reached through the monthly 21st Century Program at J.A. Fair Preparatory Academy. The museum raised $14,326 in February through donations and sponsorships, including $5,000 from Stephens Inc., $2,500 from the Legacy Capital Wealth Partners, and $1,000 from George and Linda Norton for the museum fundraiser in November. Former Commissioner Helen T. Leigh made her annual contribution of $4,500 to assist with maintenance of the museum lawn. In just the first two months of 2025 the museum has raised $16,481 towards its goal of raising $30,000 each year in outside funding. Gift shop sales for February were $573.14, which represented a 3% increase over February of last year. War Toys: Ukraine, a traveling exhibit from Exhibits USA and Mid-America Arts Alliance in Kansas City, opened on February 4, the exhibit was curated by Brian McCarty, an internationally recognized photographer who founded the nonprofit organization War Toys to address the effects of displacement and war-related trauma on children. The exhibit features photographs by McCarty in conjunction with artwork drawn by Ukrainian children in the summer of 2022 after the Russian invasion of their country a few months earlier. The exhibit will remain at the museum through August 11. The exhibit received coverage in the February 5 and February 10 issues of the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. More than 50 people attended the 2nd Annual Vintage Military Gear Show on February 16. The show featured original and reproduction memorabilia from Civil War, World Wars I and II, and Vietnam military from Arthur Eschenburg and Hayden Lang, two exhibitors from the museum’s vintage military vehicle show last October. A photograph of the event appeared in the February 17 issue of the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. In recognition of African American History Month, the Museum installed a historical marker commemorating the contributions of African American soldiers in the Civil War on February 22. The marker is located behind the museum in MacArthur Park. 55 people attended the dedication which included a program on the United States Colored Troops in Arkansas by Civil War historian Mark Christ. Among the guests were State Representative Denise Ennett and descendants of some of the soldiers who served in the USCT. News segments on the installation of the new historical marker appeared on both KARK Channel 11 and KLRT Fox 16. Links to the coverage are listed below. https://www.kark.com/video/historic-marker-unveiled-at-macarthur-military-museum-honoring-civilwar-soldiers-in-arkansas/10481267/ https://www.fox16.com/video/historic-marker-unveiled-at-macarthur-military-museum-honoring-civil-warsoldiers-in-arkansas/10481299/ Little Rock TV filmed the event, and a video is available via the link below. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KjlYFmIvyY4 The “Movies at MacArthur” film for February was rescheduled due to inclement weather. The Search for Kennedy’s PT 109 was screened on February 26 and had 52 people in attendance. The March film, The Codebreaker, is scheduled for March 18 to commemorate Women’s History Month. The documentary relates the contributions of Elizebeth Smith Friedman, the ground-breaking cryptanalyst whose painstaking work to decode thousands of messages for the U.S. government would send infamous gangsters to prison in the 1930s and bring down a massive, near-invisible Nazi spy ring in WWII. Together with her husband, the legendary cryptologist William Friedman, Elizebeth helped develop the methods that led to the creation of the powerful new science of cryptology and laid the foundation for modern codebreaking today. The museum has finalized its 2025 schedule of “On the Road with Mark 7 Christ” bus tours of Arkansas Civil War sites. The next tour is scheduled for March 22 and will feature the Camden Expedition sites. The Camden Expedition was a Federal campaign that launched from the Arsenal grounds on March 23, 1864, returning to Little Rock on May 3. It was the final campaign conducted by the Union Army in south Arkansas during the Civil War and was designed to meet up with additional Union troops in north Louisiana and invade Texas. Stops will include battle sites at Prairie D ’Ane in Prescott, Poinson Spring, Marks’ Mills and Jenkins Ferry. Lunch will be provided at the McCollum-Chidester House in Camden, General Frederick Steele’s headquarters for the two weeks he was in that town. The fall bus tour, scheduled for September 6, will include Civil War sites in the Delta, including visits to Arkansas Post and Lakeport Plantation. Two members of the museum staff – Stephan McAteer and Shane Lind – successfully completed training in the Certified Tourism Ambassador program offered by the Little Rock Convention and Visitors Bureau. In partnership with the Civil War Round Table of Arkansas the museum will host “An Evening with General Grant” on March 25 and “An Evening with President Grant” on March 26. Living Historian Dr. Curt Fields, who has portrayed General Grant in numerous films and who was selected as the official representative for the U.S. Grant Boyhood Home Association in Georgetown, Ohio, will present programs on Grant’s career as both Civil War general and President of the United States. This number included: (1) on-site visitation, (2) special events, (3) virtual programming through the museum's mini-documentaries and interviews, and (4) offsite programming and outreach. War Toys: Ukraine, a traveling exhibit from Exhibits USA and Mid-America Arts Alliance in Kansas City, continues to receive favorable responses from visitors. The exhibit features photographs by Brian McCarty, an internationally recognized photographer, in conjunction with artwork drawn by Ukrainian children in the summer of 2022 following the Russian invasion of their country a few months earlier. It will remain at the museum through August 11. Museum staff is working with staff from the Arkansas Museum of Fine Arts to develop partnership opportunities while the exhibit is in Little Rock. In celebration of March as Women's History Month, the museum featured The Codebreaker as its monthly "Movies at MacArthur" film. The documentary showcased the contributions of Elizebeth Smith Friedman, an American cryptanalyst who deciphered enemy codes in both World Wars and helped to solve international smuggling cases during Prohibition. Attendance at the March 18 screening was 74. For the first three months of 2025, attendance at the “Movies at MacArthur” program totaled 160 persons, representing a 68% increase over last year’s first quarter. Approximately 40 persons participated in a bus tour of Civil War sites associated with the Camden Expedition on March 22. The tour was led by Arkansas historian and author Mark Christ and included stops at Okolona, Prescott, Poison Spring, Camden, and Fordyce. The group enjoyed a catered meal at the historic McCollum-Chidester House in Camden. A summary of the tour was written by one of the attendees, Angie Faller, who also serves on the museum’s advisory board. In partnership with the 7 Civil War Round Table of Arkansas the museum hosted “An Evening with General Grant” on March 25 and “An Evening with President Grant” on March 26. Living Historian Dr. Curt Fields, who has portrayed General Grant in numerous films and who was selected as the official representative for the U.S. Grant Boyhood Home Association in Georgetown, Ohio, presented programs on Grant’s life as both Civil War general and President of the United States. Approximately 145 persons attended one or both nights of the program. A photo of Dr. Fields as General Grant appeared in the March 26 issue of the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. The museum will partner with the Clinton Presidential Library and Museum to celebrate Jazz Appreciation Month in April with music from the United States Air Force Band of MidAmerica. The Shades of Blue jazz ensemble will play a free concert at the Clinton Library starting at 6 pm on April 9th. The 18-piece jazz band offers something for everyone - classic and modern jazz literature; patriotic music; and some “pops” selections featuring their fantastic vocalist. The museum has begun a partnership with Freedom Sings Arkansas, a non-profit whose mission is to work with veterans and active-duty military to tell their stories through the process of songwriting. Local songwriters will meet with area veterans at the museum on the second Monday of each month starting on April 14. For more information on the organization, visit their website at: https://www.freedomsingsarkansas.org/ . We have started a new volunteer recruitment campaign called “Be a Parks Hero.” Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be 1 checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Therapeutic Recreation The TR Division will host the 23rd Annual Therapeutic Recreation Arts Festival on May 2, 2025, from 10:00am-1:00pm at the AR State Fairgrounds Hall of Industry. This annual event is in celebration of therapeutic recreation and provides a unique opportunity for the disability community to engage with children with special needs in Little Rock and across Central Arkansas by providing make it take it craft projects, games, hands-on experiences, etc. for children that attend this free event. Booths are provided by organizations, agencies, and businesses that either provide services for the disability community or have an interest in being a part of their community as a whole. This is a great way for agencies to network and for teachers and families to learn more about services available for their children. The event will include 35 booths, a magician, a photo booth, arts and crafts, recreation activities and a dance contest! **TR Youth Summer Day Camp Registration opened on April 1st. The TR Summer Day Camp will be located at Fulbright Elementary School. Enrollment is full with 19 campers registered. We do allow for a waiting list. The camp will run as follow: Monday-Friday June 9 -July 18 Time: 8:30 am-3:30 pm The Therapeutic Recreation Division uses education and recreation services to help people with disabilities develop and enhance their quality of life. This day camp is a therapeutic based program that emphasizes fun recreational activities for people with special needs to promote the development of motor skills, social skills, independence and other related areas. This camp is active, and days are filled with games, swimming, community outings, arts and crafts and more. Each child completes an assessment process and receives an Individual Recreation Plan completed by the TR staff. This plan includes goals for each camper that staff will work on intensively throughout the camp process. Progress notes are completed daily to evaluate each camper’s progress. Despite the heavy rain this month, we were able to host the US Kids Tournament on the 13th, which attracted over 80 participants, along with family and friends from across the state and nearby states. We have begun exploring the proposal for building a cart barn to house our golf carts. Director Couch, along with the designer and staff from the First Tee of Central Arkansas, have met several times regarding this project. It also involves a private donation from a family to the First Tee organization, which will help fund a pavilion on the driving range for the First Tee of Central Arkansas. We are very excited about this development. Rounds of golf continue to increase as we see many new faces visiting our facility. More people are not only practicing on the driving range but are also playing the course because they have never experienced it before. As I always say, word of mouth is critical in golf. If you have good greens and fairways, they will come. I want to give a huge shout-out to our maintenance crew and the Urban Forestry Division for their efforts in cleaning up the seven trees we lost during the storms earlier this month. This demonstrates how effective communication and teamwork can be. I would also like to recognize staff member Larry Lance for his attention to detail with the flowers around our building. Larry takes great pride in keeping the flowers healthy, watered, and trimmed. A good first impression is essential for any facility. Additionally, I want to commend staff member Jerry White, who has gone above and beyond to help pick up golf balls on the driving range, especially when we are shorthanded or preparing for an event. This level of commitment and pride is what makes having a good staff so important. The Monk Wade Junior event, hosted by the Arkansas State Golf Association, is scheduled for May 10 and 11. This is a significant junior event for Central Arkansas, bringing together over 100 youth and their families from surrounding states and throughout Arkansas for a big two-day tournament. As we continue to strive for success in 2025, I am looking forward to the coming months filled with warm days, sunshine, and happy faces. Something I love seeing every day here at First Tee. If you haven’t visited First Tee lately or ever, I invite you to come out, check out our facility, and bring your golf clubs! Rebsamen Golf There were several rainy days this month. Little Rock Open men’s professional tennis tourney is May 25-June 1, 2025. ***As a reminder, there was a fire on Wednesday, March 19 in the woods behind courts 8-12. We had to evacuate the facility around 5:00 PM as the fire approached the back of courts 9-12. Fire department were able to get the fire out right before it got to those courts. We lost a few windscreens on those courts but were overall lucky as it could have been much worse. The area is very burnt back in those woods that stretch towards Boyle Park Rd. It continued to smolder for several days but gets better each day. Museum of Arkansas Military History Museum attendance for April was 3,227. This number included: (1) on-site visitation, (2) special events, (3) virtual programming through the museum's mini-documentaries and interviews, and (4) off-site programming and outreach. On-site visitation included 624 walk-in guests and 512 visitors to special events, tours, etc. during the month. In addition to Arkansas, guests came from 27 states – Alabama, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington – as well as from Canada, England, Ireland, Germany, Guatemala, the Philippines and Switzerland. The museum's virtual documentaries/interviews received 1031 views in April including more than 450 views of the two presentations by Dr. Curt Fields as General and President Grant on March 25 and 26. Off-site programming reached 275 children at the Dunbar and Stephens Community Centers and the J.A. Fair Preparatory Academy. Additional off-site special events included the Mobile City Hall on April 7, the “Shades of Blue” concert at the Clinton Presidential Center on April 9, and the QQA Preview Party on April 14. For the first four months of 2025 the museum has raised $22,421 through donations and sponsorships, which is 74% of the annual goal of raising $30,000. Gift shop sales for April were $931.76 for a total of $3146.61 so far this year. War Toys: Ukraine, a traveling exhibit from Exhibits USA and Mid-America Arts Alliance in Kansas City, has been extended through September 28. The exhibit features photographs by Brian McCarty in conjunction with artwork drawn by Ukrainian children in the summer of 2022 following the Russian invasion. Museum staff have finalized partnership opportunities with staff from the Arkansas Museum of Fine Arts to host field trips to the exhibit by students in its summer programs as well as a panel discussion featuring Brian McCarty on September 18 at AMFA. David Collins joined the museum staff as Museum Program Assistant on April 7. Mr. Collins has a Bachelor of Science in Education degree from UCA with a major in Secondary Social Studies. He has over six years of experience teaching in schools in Central Arkansas, most recently as the EAST facilitator at 8 Lonoke Public School District. He also has a Master of Arts in History from UCA and a Master of Arts in Public History from UALR. His museum/preservation experience includes serving as the Planning and Preservation Coordinator at the Capitol Zoning District Commission from 2019-2021 and the Public Programs Manager at Historic Cane Hill 2021-2023, where he developed and presented educational programming. His depth of experience will make him an asset to the museum. The April "Movies at MacArthur" film, Model T’s to War: Ambulances on the Western Front, had attendance of 56 guests on April 15. Attendance at the monthly program for the first four months of 2025 has been 216. The film series is 68% ahead of last year’s attendance and is on track to have another record-breaking year. The May "Movies at MacArthur" film, War Letters, is scheduled for May 20. The museum will offer two hours of PD credit to teachers who attend the movie and participate in a discussion forum with Museum Program Assistant David Collins. The museum hosted the final meeting of the Aesthetic Club's 2024-2025 season on April 22. Approximately 85 members attended. The organization will take a summer hiatus before resuming its meetings in October. The women's club has held its meetings at the Arsenal Building since 1894 and makes an annual contribution to the museum. The museum partnered with the Clinton Presidential Library and Museum to celebrate Jazz Appreciation Month on April 9 with music from the United States Air Force Band of Mid-America. The Shades of Blue jazz ensemble played a free concert at the Clinton Library to over 325 people. The museum hosted the first meeting of Freedom Sings Arkansas on April 14. The non-profit's mission is to work with veterans and active-duty military to tell their stories through the process of songwriting. Local songwriters will meet with area veterans at the museum on the second Monday of each month. For more information on the organization, visit their website at: https://www.freedomsingsarkansas.org/ . The museum hosted the Arkansas State Archives’ Spring symposium, Lost Utopias: The Search for Arkansas’s Vanished Tourist Attractions, on April 26. The event included presentations on Monte Ne, the history of Dogpatch USA, Hot Springs’ forgotten attractions, and the history of Arkansas tourism to its natural springs. The event was free to the public. To commemorate the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War, the museum hosted Lieutenant Colonel Ret. Hugh Mills Jr. for a program on April 29. A native of Hot Springs, Mills is one of the most decorated helicopter pilots in the Vietnam War and is the author of Low-Level Hell, A Scout Pilot in the Big Red One, which recounts his experiences in Vietnam. He discussed his experiences in the Vietnam War as well as his twenty-six year-career in the United States Army. Registration has opened for the 2025 MacArthur Park “History on the Run” 5k race on May 2. The race will begin and end in front of the museum and take runners and walkers through the MacArthur Park and Pettaway Park neighborhoods. Approximately 115 runners/walkers have already registered, including four corporate teams each from the UALR Bowen School of Law and L'Oreal. The museum will be a participating site in the Quapaw Quarter Association's 60th Spring Tour of Homes on May 10-11. This year's tour will focus on the MacArthur Park Historic District. The museum will appear in all publicity and promotional material for the tour. The museum will also, partner with the Clinton Presidential Library and Museum to open its America 250 celebrations on July 4, 2025, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. The celebration will include free admission at the presidential center all day followed by a Revolutionary battle reenactment on the east lawn. The event is a presented in partnership with the Daughters of the American Revolution, the Early "Arkansaw" Reenactors Association, the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History, and Blue Bell Creameries. Blue Bell Creameries will provide ice cream for the event. Therapeutic Recreation The TR Division will host the 23rd Annual Therapeutic Recreation Arts Festival on May 2, 2025, from 10:00am-1:00pm at the AR State Fairgrounds Hall of Industry. This annual event is in celebration of therapeutic recreation and provides a unique opportunity for the disability community to engage with children with special needs in Little Rock and across Central Arkansas by providing make it take it craft projects, games, hands-on experiences, etc. for children that attend this free event. Booths are provided by organizations, agencies, and businesses that either provide services for the disability community or have an interest in being a part of their community as a whole. This is a great way for agencies to network and for teachers and families to learn more about services available for their children. The event will include 35 booths, a magician, a photo booth, arts and crafts, recreation activities and a dance contest! **TR Youth Summer Day Camp Registration opened on April 1st. The TR Summer Day Camp will be located at Fulbright Elementary School. Enrollment is full with 19 campers registered. We do allow for a waiting list. The camp will run as follow: Monday-Friday June 9 -July 18 Time: 8:30 am-3:30 pm The Therapeutic Recreation Division uses education and recreation services to help people with disabilities develop and enhance their quality of life. This day camp is a therapeutic based program that emphasizes fun recreational activities for people with special needs to promote the development of motor skills, social skills, independence and other related areas. This camp is active, and days are filled with games, swimming, community outings, arts and crafts and more. Each child completes an assessment process and receives an Individual Recreation Plan completed by the TR staff. This plan includes goals for each camper that staff will work on intensively throughout the camp process. Progress notes are completed daily to evaluate each camper’s progress. It continued to smolder for several days but gets better each day. Museum of Arkansas Military History Museum attendance for April was 3,227. This number included: (1) on-site visitation, (2) special events, (3) virtual programming through the museum's mini-documentaries and interviews, and (4) off-site programming and outreach. On-site visitation included 624 walk-in guests and 512 visitors to special events, tours, etc. during the month. In addition to Arkansas, guests came from 27 states – Alabama, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington – as well as from Canada, England, Ireland, Germany, Guatemala, the Philippines and Switzerland. The museum's virtual documentaries/interviews received 1031 views in April including more than 450 views of the two presentations by Dr. Curt Fields as General and President Grant on March 25 and 26. Off-site programming reached 275 children at the Dunbar and Stephens Community Centers and the J.A. Fair Preparatory Academy. Additional off-site special events included the Mobile City Hall on April 7, the “Shades of Blue” concert at the Clinton Presidential Center on April 9, and the QQA Preview Party on April 14. For the first four months of 2025 the museum has raised $22,421 through donations and sponsorships, which is 74% of the annual goal of raising $30,000. Gift shop sales for April were $931.76 for a total of $3146.61 so far this year. War Toys: Ukraine, a traveling exhibit from Exhibits USA and Mid-America Arts Alliance in Kansas City, has been extended through September 28. The exhibit features photographs by Brian McCarty in conjunction with artwork drawn by Ukrainian children in the summer of 2022 following the Russian invasion. Museum staff have finalized partnership opportunities with staff from the Arkansas Museum of Fine Arts to host field trips to the exhibit by students in its summer programs as well as a panel discussion featuring Brian McCarty on September 18 at AMFA. David Collins joined the museum staff as Museum Program Assistant on April 7. Mr. Collins has a Bachelor of Science in Education degree from UCA with a major in Secondary Social Studies. He has over six years of experience teaching in schools in Central Arkansas, most recently as the EAST facilitator at 8 Lonoke Public School District. He also has a Master of Arts in History from UCA and a Master of Arts in Public History from UALR. His museum/preservation experience includes serving as the Planning and Preservation Coordinator at the Capitol Zoning District Commission from 2019-2021 and the Public Programs Manager at Historic Cane Hill 2021-2023, where he developed and presented educational programming. His depth of experience will make him an asset to the museum. The April "Movies at MacArthur" film, Model T’s to War: Ambulances on the Western Front, had attendance of 56 guests on April 15. Attendance at the monthly program for the first four months of 2025 has been 216. The film series is 68% ahead of last year’s attendance and is on track to have another record-breaking year. The May "Movies at MacArthur" film, War Letters, is scheduled for May 20. The museum will offer two hours of PD credit to teachers who attend the movie and participate in a discussion forum with Museum Program Assistant David Collins. The museum hosted the final meeting of the Aesthetic Club's 2024-2025 season on April 22. Approximately 85 members attended. The organization will take a summer hiatus before resuming its meetings in October. The women's club has held its meetings at the Arsenal Building since 1894 and makes an annual contribution to the museum. The museum partnered with the Clinton Presidential Library and Museum to celebrate Jazz Appreciation Month on April 9 with music from the United States Air Force Band of Mid-America. The Shades of Blue jazz ensemble played a free concert at the Clinton Library to over 325 people. The museum hosted the first meeting of Freedom Sings Arkansas on April 14. The non-profit's mission is to work with veterans and active-duty military to tell their stories through the process of songwriting. Local songwriters will meet with area veterans at the museum on the second Monday of each month. For more information on the organization, visit their website at: https://www.freedomsingsarkansas.org/ . The museum hosted the Arkansas State Archives’ Spring symposium, Lost Utopias: The Search for Arkansas’s Vanished Tourist Attractions, on April 26. The event included presentations on Monte Ne, the history of Dogpatch USA, Hot Springs’ forgotten attractions, and the history of Arkansas tourism to its natural springs. The event was free to the public. To commemorate the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War, the museum hosted Lieutenant Colonel Ret. Hugh Mills Jr. for a program on April 29. A native of Hot Springs, Mills is one of the most decorated helicopter pilots in the Vietnam War and is the author of Low-Level Hell, A Scout Pilot in the Big Red One, which recounts his experiences in Vietnam. He discussed his experiences in the Vietnam War as well as his twenty-six year-career in the United States Army. Registration has opened for the 2025 MacArthur Park “History on the Run” 5k race on May 2. The race will begin and end in front of the museum and take runners and walkers through the MacArthur Park and Pettaway Park neighborhoods. Approximately 115 runners/walkers have already registered, including four corporate teams each from the UALR Bowen School of Law and L'Oreal. The museum will be a participating site in the Quapaw Quarter Association's 60th Spring Tour of Homes on May 10-11. This year's tour will focus on the MacArthur Park Historic District. The museum will appear in all publicity and promotional material for the tour. The museum will also, partner with the Clinton Presidential Library and Museum to open its America 250 celebrations on July 4, 2025, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. The celebration will include free admission at the presidential center all day followed by a Revolutionary battle reenactment on the east lawn. The event is a presented in partnership with the Daughters of the American Revolution, the Early "Arkansaw" Reenactors Association, the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History, and Blue Bell Creameries. Blue Bell Creameries will provide ice cream for the event. Special Tours at the Museum in April included: (1) senior group from Our Lady of Souls Church on April 10, (2) special needs elementary students from Stephens and Terry Elementary Schools on April 17, (3) 9 University of Central Arkansas's ROTC program on April 24, (4) two groups of 3rd grade students from Ridge Road Elementary in North Little Rock on April 25, and (5) students from Mountain Home Christian Academy on April 25. Volunteer Division June 2025 The Volunteer Coordinator attended the largest conference on volunteerism, Points of Light, from June 3rd – 6th. We have started a new volunteer recruitment campaign called “Be a Parks Hero.” Jr. Park Ranger Day Camp dates: June 9th-13th June 23rd – 27th July 7th – 11th Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that park is not already under a contract. 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects 1 We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. Volunteer Division July 2025 We have 16 new Jr. Park Rangers. The first week of camp had to be cancelled due to sickness but the other two weeks were a hot success. National Public Lands Day – Sept. 27th; Hindman Park; 9 am Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that park is not already under a contract. 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 1 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. We need help mapping them using iNaturalist and removing them/cutting them back. Sign up at www.littlerock.gov/volunteer. Any volunteer opportunity working with a vulnerable population (children, senior citizens, etc.) must pass a background check. Parks pays for it. Questions? This plan builds upon decades of thoughtful planning, incorporating insights from the 2001 and 2020 Master Plans, Youth Master Plan, Downtown Little Rock Master Plan, Complete Streets Master Plan, the Parks Sustainability Guidelines, and the 3-Year Age-Friendly Action Plan. By aligning these foundational efforts with the latest CAPRA National Accreditation Standards and the City of Little Rock’s Core Values, this strategic plan offers a forward-thinking, community-focused framework that ensures equity, innovation, and accountability remain at the heart of our work. This plan is organized around five key goals: enhancing community health and quality of life, fostering environmental resilience, creating inclusive and accessible parks, expanding outdoor recreation opportunities, and strengthening partnerships and community engagement. Each goal is supported by actionable objectives and a detailed timeline, reflecting our commitment to transparency and measurable outcomes. Together, these efforts position Little Rock as a model city for sustainable, inclusive, and innovative park management, delivering exceptional service to every corner of our community. Volunteer Division September 2025 National Public Lands Day – Sept. 27th; Hindman Park; 9 am Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that park is not already under a contract. 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. We need help mapping them using iNaturalist and removing them/cutting them back. 1 Sign up at www.littlerock.gov/volunteer. Any volunteer opportunity working with a vulnerable population (children, senior citizens, etc.) must pass a background check. Parks pays for it. Questions? To volunteer at a brick and mortar, contact that facility directly. To volunteer for the adoption programs, #LRParksPushyPlants, Eagle Scouts, clean-ups or VPR, contact ksykes@littlerock.gov. For Marathon, contact glamm@littlerock.gov. 2

Volunteer Division October 2025 Thank you to our chair, Ben France, along with the Mayor, Vice-Mayor and Dir. Joan Adcock for their support at Hindman Park on National Public Lands Day. Also a big thank you to our staff in Operations, Outdoor Recreation and Marketing who helped prepare for the day. Thank you to Starbucks too for donating coffee. We had about 35 volunteers. They painted the benches, bleachers and basketball goal posts. The baseball field fence is now clear of trees and other vegetation and can be repaired by staff. They also weedeated around the baseball field and the entire disc golf course. A lot of downed limbs were picked up and piled up at the curb along with trash bags. The volunteers were so proud and happy with their accomplishments and ecstatic when Taziki’s showed up. New friendships were forged; we strengthened community that day! Dir. Adcock said that the park hasn’t looked that good in years. Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that park is not already under a contract. 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 1 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. We need help mapping them using iNaturalist and removing them/cutting them back. Sign up at www.littlerock.gov/volunteer. Any volunteer opportunity working with a vulnerable population (children, senior citizens, etc.) must pass a background check. Parks pays for it. Questions? To volunteer at a brick and mortar, contact that facility directly. To volunteer for the adoption programs, #LRParksPushyPlants, Eagle Scouts, clean-ups or VPR, contact ksykes@littlerock.gov. For Marathon, contact glamm@littlerock.gov. 2

Working on bids for the 2026 junior Tournament schedule. Museum of Arkansas Military History Museum attendance for October was 4,224. This number includes : (1) on-site visitation, (2) special events, (3) virtual programming through the museum's mini-documentaries and interviews, and (4) offsite programming and outreach. Volunteer Division November 2025 Compared to Quarter 1 – Quarter 3 in 2024, volunteerism in Parks and Recreation is up 6%. Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that park is not already under a contract. 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. We need help mapping them using iNaturalist and removing them/cutting them back. 1 Sign up at www.littlerock.gov/volunteer. Any volunteer opportunity working with a vulnerable population (children, senior citizens, etc.) must pass a background check. Parks pays for it. Questions? To volunteer at a brick and mortar, contact that facility directly. To volunteer for the adoption programs, #LRParksPushyPlants, Eagle Scouts, clean-ups or VPR, contact ksykes@littlerock.gov. For Marathon, contact glamm@littlerock.gov. 2

Volunteer Division December 2025 The Commission’s interest in adopting a park is greatly appreciated. The recommended process is for the Commission to adopt a park and conduct an organized, monthly group cleanup or Commissioners can volunteer monthly at their leisure. For example, one commissioner might volunteer for 30 minutes one day while another one volunteers for 30 minutes another day. Adopt-a-Park Requirements 1) Volunteer at least 2 hours a month either as an organized event or individually at your leisure. 2) Parks provides tools such as weed eaters, loppers, shovels, and rakes. We also provide litter grabbers and trash bags. 3) Volunteers receive a free pavilion rental per calendar year. 4) Volunteers receive a sign with their name on it. 5) Hours are turned in by the end of each month. Park Adoption Recommendations 1) Kanis Park 2) War Memorial Park Volunteer Opportunities 1) Volunteer Park Ranger (VPR) VPR’s are ambassadors, stewards and protectors of our park system. They officially represent the city, beautify our parks and are extended eyes and ears for the LRPD and Parks. Uniforms and training are free and VPR’s are expected to volunteer for 16 hrs./month. 2) Adopt-A-Park, Trail or Flowerbed We have over 50 open spaced parks, over 20 miles of soft surface trails and ~30 flowerbeds. Adopters spend at least 2 hrs./month in their adopted area. Tools can be checked out and trash bags, flowers, mulch and soil are free. Adopters receive a sign with their name/org. on it and one free pavilion rental per calendar year. 3) Park or Trail Clean-up An org/individual/family can schedule a clean-up by contacting Karen at ksykes@littlerock.gov. We ask that all vols schedule with us to ensure that the park is not already under a contract. 1 4) Jim Daily Aquatic and Fitness Center We need volunteer fitness instructors to expand our programming. 5) Rebsamen and First Tee Golf Courses Vols marshal, clean golf carts, pick up balls, etc. 6) Community Centers Vols are needed to coach various sports programs and help with special events. 7) Eagle Scout Projects We have various projects that Eagle Scouts can work towards. 8) Marathon Vols are needed to help with their races throughout the year. 9) #LRParksPushyPlants Parks has committed to removing 10%/year of our invasive species. We need help mapping them using iNaturalist and removing them/cutting them back. Sign up at www.littlerock.gov/volunteer. Any volunteer opportunity working with a vulnerable population (children, senior citizens, etc.) must pass a background check. Parks pays for it. Questions? To volunteer at a brick and mortar, contact that facility directly. To volunteer for the adoption programs, #LRParksPushyPlants, Eagle Scouts, clean-ups or VPR, contact ksykes@littlerock.gov. For Marathon, contact glamm@littlerock.gov. 2
